lectures.title: Insert Method Binary Tree using Array

cues.en: Now in this lecture we are going to look at insert method for binary tree using array implementation.
So in the previous lecture we have created the binary tree class as an empty binary tree.
So we have array and let's use index.
So the next thing that we are going to do we are going to declare the insert method inside the binary
tree class.
So it's obvious that as a parameter it's going to take value.
Then the next thing that we are going to do, we are going to take this value and assign it to the next
cell in this array.
So we know that last used index saves the last used cell's index.
So if we put plus one and assign the value it's going to insert this node to the next cell.
Then it's obvious that we have to increase the last used index by one.
Because in this case if we insert one more element, the last used index will be increased.
Now let's look at how this is going to work.
So let's say we want to insert n one.
So if we pass n one over here and the last use index is zero.
It's going to insert this n1 at the index of one in this array.
So as we mentioned before, we are not using the zeroth index for making our calculation easier.
That's why it's going to be inserted at the index of one.
Then if you call this insert method one more time for example for n2, the next thing that it's going
to do, it's going to insert n2 to the next cell, which is going to be the index of two.
Because here in this case the last used index was one.
So one plus one is equal to two.
So it's inserted at the index of two.
And the last use index increased by one becomes two.
Now if we continue to insert one more element in this case n3.
So here it's going to come over here and insert it at the index of three.
Because last used index is two.
And plus one is going to be three.
And this is going to be inserted at the index of three.
And the last use index will be increased to the three because in this case the last use index is going
to be the index of three, which is n three.
So that's how the logic looks like in this case.
